md: A **monomer** is a small molecule that can join to others like it. A **polymer** is the very long chain molecule formed when thousands of monomers join. The process is called **addition polymerisation**, and the scheme gives a mark for each word: *addition* because the monomers simply add on to one another and nothing else is made, *polymerisation* because a polymer is the result.

prompt: Ethene molecules join together to make poly(ethene). What is the full name of this process?
explain: Addition polymerisation. Writing polymerisation on its own earns one of the two marks; addition is the other.

text: 2. Naming a polymer from its monomer

md: The polymer's name is built from the monomer's: write **poly**, then the monomer's name **in brackets**. Ethene gives **poly(ethene)**, which the scheme also accepts as polythene. **Chloroethene**, whose older name is vinyl chloride, gives **poly(chloroethene)**, sold as PVC. Poly(ethene) makes carrier bags, bottles and cling film; PVC makes window frames, drainpipes and the insulation on electric cables.

title: One rule, one mark
md: Summer 2025's C2 Foundation report records that naming the polymer made from ethene was beyond most candidates, and that many left the line blank. It is a rule to learn, not chemistry to work out.

md: When one of the two bonds in a C=C opens, each carbon is left with a bond to spare, and that bond links it to the next monomer. That is why every monomer for addition polymerisation is an **alkene**, or has a C=C like one. An alkane has only single bonds, each already in use, so it has nothing to open and **cannot** form an addition polymer.

title: Why nothing else is made
md: The monomers only add on to one another: no atom leaves and no second product forms. So the polymer holds every atom of every monomer, which is the idea behind the atom-count check in section 5.

prompt: Ethene and ethane both have two carbon atoms. Why can ethene form an addition polymer when ethane cannot?
options: ethene has a C=C, and one of its two bonds can open to link to the next molecule
ethene has more hydrogen atoms to give away
ethane molecules are too large to join together
answer: ethene has a C=C, and one of its two bonds can open to link to the next molecule
explain: The C=C. Opening one of its two bonds gives each carbon a spare bond to link with; ethane's bonds are all single and all in use.

md:
**The question.** Write the equation for the polymerisation of ethene. **[2]**
**Step 1 — draw the monomer.** Ethene, with its C=C and all four hydrogens, and **n** in front: n molecules go in.
**Step 2 — open the double bond.** Redraw the two carbons joined by a **single** bond, with every hydrogen where it was.

prompt: In the repeat unit drawn above, count the bonds around one carbon atom, including the bond that passes through the bracket. How many are there?
explain: Four: two to hydrogens, one to the other carbon and one through the bracket to the next unit. If you had kept the double bond you would count five, which is how that mistake gets caught.

md:
**Step 3 — show the chain carrying on.** Draw a bond out of each carbon, through a **square bracket** on each side.
**Step 4 — add n.** Write **n** after the closing bracket: the unit repeats n times, once for each monomer. The scheme gives one mark for the structure and one for n on both sides of the arrow.

Chloroethene is $\ce{C2H3Cl}$, so the repeat unit of poly(chloroethene) is $\ce{C2H3Cl}$ as well, with the same relative formula mass. Check every repeat unit you draw twice: the **same atoms** as the monomer, and **four bonds** at every carbon.

prompt: The repeat unit of poly(chloroethene) is drawn above. How many hydrogen atoms does it contain?
explain: 3, the same as in chloroethene. The chlorine took the place of one of ethene's four hydrogens, and nothing was lost when the monomers joined.

md: Mark off **two neighbouring carbons** that repeat along the chain: each monomer brought two. Remove the two bonds that join that unit to its neighbours, then **put the double bond back** between its carbons, keeping every group where it was. Here each unit carries three hydrogens and a $\ce{CH3}$ group, so the monomer is **propene**, $\ce{C3H6}$.

title: GCSE Chemistry Revision "Addition Polymers" (Triple)
why: A second run through monomers, the repeat unit and how the equation is drawn.

prompt: In the polymer chain drawn above, every second carbon carries a CH₃ group. Name the monomer the chain was made from.
explain: Propene: put the double bond back into one two-carbon unit and count three carbons in all. Propane has no double bond, so it could never have polymerised.

md:
explain how **monomers** join into a very long chain molecule, a **polymer**, and call the process **addition polymerisation**.
name the polymer from its monomer: **poly(ethene)** from ethene, **poly(chloroethene)** from chloroethene.
draw a repeat unit with **brackets**, a bond through each, a **single** C–C bond and **n**, and write the equation with n on both sides.
check a repeat unit: the **same atoms** as the monomer, and four bonds at every carbon.
work back from a section of chain to its monomer by putting the **C=C** back.

Polymers sit inside the organic chemistry question of the C2 paper. The first mark is usually a name: the process, or the polymer made from a named monomer. At Higher the last marks are a drawing: a repeat unit or a structural equation, with n on both sides. Stuck on a drawing? Draw the monomer, open its double bond, then count four bonds at every carbon. The Sheet below lists the traps.
